case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Quiet Title Act's 12-year statute of limitations constitutes a jurisdictional requirement that strips federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction, or merely a claim-processing rule subject to equitable exceptions such as tolling and waiver.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Quiet Title Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g), which establishes a 12-year deadline for bringing '[a]ny civil action under' the Act, with an explicit exception for actions brought by a State, in the context of the federal government's sovereign immunity waiver for property title disputes.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners Larry Steven Wilkins and Jane B. Stanton, represented by Pacific Legal Foundation, argue that the QTA's statute of limitations is a non-jurisdictional claim-processing rule rather than a jurisdictional bar. Under this interpretation, the 12-year deadline would be subject to equitable doctrines such as tolling, waiver, and forfeiture, allowing courts to consider untimely claims under appropriate circumstances. Petitioners contend that treating the limitations period as merely a claim-processing rule aligns with the Supreme Court's modern framework distinguishing true jurisdictional requirements from procedural filing rules, and that Congress did not clearly and explicitly designate the QTA's time limit as jurisdictional.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States, represented by Solicitor General Elizabeth B. Prelogar, argues that the QTA's 12-year statute of limitations is jurisdictional in nature because it is embedded within the federal government's waiver of sovereign immunity. The government contends that waivers of sovereign immunity must be strictly construed, and that the time limitation is an integral condition of that waiver — meaning that failure to comply with the deadline deprives federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction entirely. Under this view, the limitations period cannot be tolled or waived, and courts must dismiss untimely claims for lack of jurisdiction regardless of equitable considerations.
key_precedents: Tobar v. United States, 639 F.3d 1191 (9th Cir. 2011) — establishing that waiver of sovereign immunity is a prerequisite to federal-court jurisdiction
Maya v. Centex Corp., 658 F.3d 1060 (9th Cir. 2011) — addressing the distinction between Rule 12(b)(1) jurisdictional challenges and Rule 12(b)(6) claim-processing challenges
Caltex Plastics, Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 824 F.3d 1156 (9th Cir. 2016) — governing standards for Rule 12(b)(6) motions to dismiss
Parrino v. FHP, Inc., 146 F.3d 699 (9th Cir. 1998) — addressing documents a court may consider in resolving motions to dismiss
Steinle v. City & County of San Francisco, 919 F.3d 1154 (9th Cir. 2019) — recognizing supersession of Parrino on non-relevant grounds
Quiet Title Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2409a — the primary statutory framework governing the entire dispute
Congressional Research Service Report on Federal Land Ownership (Carol Hardy Vincent & Laura A. Hanson) — contextual authority regarding federal land dominance in the western United States

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas continues to press the strongest opposing argument — that the 12-year period is textually embedded within the waiver provision itself, making it constitutive of consent rather than merely procedural — and I acknowledge this structural point has genuine force that distinguishes the QTA from the FTCA at issue in Kwai Fun Wong. However, Justice Barrett's analysis is ultimately more persuasive: the Court's post-Arbaugh framework requires a clear statement before treating any deadline as jurisdictional, and that analytical discipline applies even in the sovereign immunity context as Kwai Fun Wong explicitly held. The fact that Block and Mottaz treated § 2409a(g) as jurisdictional cannot be dispositive when those decisions predated the Court's systematic course correction — they reflect the old reflexive approach the Court has since deliberately abandoned, and while I would not formally overrule them, their reasoning on the jurisdictional question has been substantially undermined. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with instructions to write narrowly: hold only that § 2409a(g) is a non-jurisdictional claim-processing rule under the modern clear-statement framework, expressly reserve the question of the precise scope of equitable tolling available against the government, and avoid broad pronouncements about sovereign immunity doctrine that could destabilize adjacent areas of law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument — that my own textualist and originalist methodology cuts against me because § 2409a(g) does not speak in jurisdictional terms — is the most sophisticated challenge, and I have wrestled with it seriously. However, I remain unpersuaded for this reason: the founding-era principle of strict construction of sovereign immunity waivers is not merely a background canon but a structural constitutional principle about the separation of powers, and when Congress embeds a time limit within the waiver provision itself — as opposed to attaching it externally as in the FTCA — the original public meaning of that structure is that the time limit defines the scope of consent, not merely the procedure for exercising it. Kwai Fun Wong addressed a structurally different statute where the limitations period was not constitutive of the waiver, and the Court's post-Arbaugh clear-statement framework, while I respect its discipline, was developed in the context of ordinary statutory schemes and cannot simply override the foundational constitutional principle that courts must strictly construe the terms on which sovereigns consent to suit. Block v. North Dakota and Mottaz addressed this specific provision and remain controlling unless expressly overruled, and the majority's approach of treating them as merely superseded by doctrinal trajectory — without formally overruling them — is precisely the kind of unprincipled erosion of precedent through implication that I have consistently criticized.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's invocation of Kwai Fun Wong remains the most formidable challenge to my position, and I acknowledge its force — but I cannot accept that a post-2010 decision about the FTCA silently abrogates Block v. North Dakota's explicit holding about this specific statutory provision without the Court expressly saying so. My colleagues across the bench treat Kwai Fun Wong as effectively overruling Block and Mottaz sub silentio, but that is not how stare decisis works: when the Court has specifically addressed a particular statute's limitations period and called it jurisdictional, a later general-framework case does not automatically displace that specific holding unless it expressly addresses and overrules it. Justice Thomas correctly identifies the structural distinction that my colleagues elide — the QTA's 12-year period is not merely appended to a pre-existing waiver but is textually constitutive of the waiver itself, meaning Congress defined its consent to suit as extending only to claims brought within that window, which is precisely the kind of condition that sovereign immunity doctrine requires courts to honor strictly. I maintain my position that § 2409a(g) is jurisdictional, though I acknowledge the modern framework creates genuine tension that the Court will eventually need to resolve by either expressly overruling Block or distinguishing it on principled grounds.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas makes the strongest opposing argument by invoking Mottaz and Block v. North Dakota for the proposition that limitations periods within sovereign immunity waivers are jurisdictional conditions on consent — but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, Kwai Fun Wong explicitly held that 'it makes no difference' whether a time bar conditions a sovereign immunity waiver, because the modern clear-statement framework applies regardless of that context. The government's position fundamentally conflates two analytically distinct questions: whether the sovereign immunity waiver itself is jurisdictional (yes) and whether the embedded limitations period carries that same jurisdictional character (not automatically). Justice Thomas's reliance on Block and Mottaz cannot survive the Court's post-2010 course correction, which Boechler crystallized — those cases predated the Court's systematic effort to police the jurisdictional/claim-processing distinction, and we should not treat pre-Arbaugh precedents as controlling when the Court has since established a demanding clear-statement rule. The State carve-out in § 2409a(g) further undermines the jurisdictional reading: true jurisdictional limits do not ordinarily admit of ad hoc statutory exceptions, and Congress's deliberate choice to exempt States signals procedural calibration rather than a definition of judicial power.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas continues to press the strongest opposing argument — that Block v. North Dakota and Mottaz are controlling precedents that explicitly treated § 2409a(g) as jurisdictional, and that the 12-year period is constitutive of the waiver rather than merely procedural. I take this structural argument seriously, but as Justice Barrett persuasively explains, the Court's post-Arbaugh framework was specifically designed to correct the reflexive jurisdictional labeling that characterized those earlier decisions, and Kwai Fun Wong directly held that the sovereign immunity context does not automatically render a limitations period jurisdictional — that holding cannot be squared with treating Block and Mottaz as fully controlling on the jurisdictional question. Justice Thomas's distinction between the QTA and the FTCA — arguing the 12-year period is textually embedded within the waiver itself — is the most interesting structural argument in this case, but it proves too much: virtually any limitations period in a sovereign immunity waiver statute could be characterized as 'constitutive' of the waiver on that logic, which would effectively nullify Kwai Fun Wong's sovereign immunity holding. The text of § 2409a(g) simply does not speak in jurisdictional terms, and the State carve-out — as Justices Gorsuch and Sotomayor both note — is far more consistent with a claim-processing rule than with a hard boundary on judicial power.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas continues to press the most formidable opposing argument — that the 12-year period in § 2409a(g) is textually embedded within the waiver provision itself, making it constitutive of consent rather than merely procedural. This is a serious structural point that I do not dismiss lightly. However, as Justice Barrett correctly identifies, this argument impermissibly collapses two analytically distinct inquiries: the jurisdictional nature of the sovereign immunity waiver itself and the separate question of whether every procedural condition attached to that waiver automatically carries jurisdictional weight. Kwai Fun Wong directly addressed this conflation and rejected it, holding that the sovereign immunity context 'makes no difference' to the clear-statement analysis — and as a textualist I am bound by that holding because § 2409a(g)'s text simply does not speak in jurisdictional terms or reference subject-matter jurisdiction. Justice Alito's point that Block and Mottaz have not been formally overruled deserves acknowledgment, but those pre-Arbaugh precedents were decided before the Court established its systematic clear-statement framework, and Kwai Fun Wong's explicit application of that framework to sovereign immunity waivers substantially narrows their precedential force on the precise jurisdictional-versus-claim-processing question without requiring formal overruling.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas continues to press the strongest opposing argument — that Block v. North Dakota and Mottaz explicitly treated § 2409a(g) as jurisdictional and that the 12-year period is constitutive of the waiver rather than merely procedural. I take seriously his structural point that the QTA's limitations period is textually embedded within the waiver provision itself, which distinguishes it from the FTCA context in Kwai Fun Wong. However, as Justice Barrett correctly identifies, the analytical move Justice Thomas makes — collapsing the jurisdictional nature of the waiver itself into the separate question of whether every procedural condition attached to that waiver automatically strips courts of jurisdiction — is precisely the error the post-Arbaugh framework was designed to correct. The fact that Block and Mottaz predate the Court's systematic course correction in Arbaugh, Reed Elsevier, and Boechler, combined with Kwai Fun Wong's explicit holding that sovereign immunity context alone does not render a limitations period jurisdictional, leaves me comfortable that the modern clear-statement rule governs here and § 2409a(g) does not satisfy it.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most compelling argument remains that the 12-year period in § 2409a(g) is textually embedded within the waiver provision itself, making it constitutive of consent rather than merely procedural — but as I explained in round one, this structural observation, while accurate, does not resolve the jurisdictional question under the Court's modern framework. Kwai Fun Wong explicitly held that the sovereign immunity context 'makes no difference' to the jurisdictional inquiry, and that holding was not limited to general waiver statutes like the FTCA; it established a categorical rule that the clear-statement requirement applies regardless of whether a time bar conditions a sovereign immunity waiver. Justice Thomas's distinction between the QTA and the FTCA is textually interesting but legally insufficient — Kwai Fun Wong's reasoning rested on the analytical separation between the waiver's jurisdictional character and the limitations period's procedural character, a distinction that applies with equal force here. The State carve-out, as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor correctly observe, further confirms that Congress was engaged in procedural calibration rather than defining the outer bounds of judicial power, since true jurisdictional limits do not ordinarily admit of ad hoc statutory exceptions crafted for policy reasons.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most compelling argument remains that the 12-year period is textually embedded within the waiver provision itself, making it constitutive of consent rather than merely procedural — but as Justice Barrett correctly identifies, this analytical move conflates two distinct questions: whether the sovereign immunity waiver is jurisdictional (yes) and whether every procedural condition attached to that waiver automatically carries jurisdictional weight (not under post-2010 doctrine). Kwai Fun Wong directly addressed this precise conflation and rejected it, holding that the sovereign immunity context 'makes no difference' to the jurisdictional inquiry under the modern clear-statement framework — and that holding postdates and effectively narrows Block and Mottaz without requiring us to formally overrule them. Justice Thomas's structural argument about the State carve-out actually reinforces my position, as Justice Gorsuch observes: genuine jurisdictional limits defining the outer bounds of judicial power do not ordinarily admit of ad hoc statutory exceptions, whereas Congress's deliberate calibration of the limitations period to exempt States signals a claim-processing rule subject to legislative modification. The text of § 2409a(g) simply does not speak in unmistakably jurisdictional terms, and the Court's demanding clear-statement requirement — which Justice Thomas's own textualist methodology should honor — cannot be satisfied by structural inference alone.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Court's modern framework, crystallized in Boechler v. Commissioner (2022) and Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center (2013), requires that Congress 'speak clearly' to imbue a procedural deadline with jurisdictional consequences, and the QTA's 12-year limitation in § 2409a(g) does not plainly satisfy that standard. While the government's sovereign immunity argument has force, the Court has repeatedly cautioned against reflexively treating limitations periods embedded in statutory waivers as jurisdictional — the mere fact that a time limit conditions a waiver of sovereign immunity does not automatically make it jurisdictional under Reed Elsevier and Kwai Fun Wong. Treating the QTA's deadline as a non-jurisdictional claim-processing rule is the narrower ground for decision, consistent with my preference for minimalist rulings that avoid sweeping pronouncements about sovereign immunity doctrine, and it preserves equitable flexibility without categorically foreclosing the government's ability to raise timeliness as a defense. The structural argument that the State exception in § 2409a(g) signals jurisdictional intent is not sufficiently clear to overcome the Court's strong modern presumption against jurisdictional treatment absent explicit congressional designation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g) embeds the 12-year limitations period directly within the sovereign immunity waiver itself, and the original public meaning of sovereign immunity doctrine — well established at the founding — holds that the sovereign cannot be sued except on the precise terms it consents to be sued. As this Court stated in United States v. Mottaz, 'when waiver legislation contains a statute of limitations, the limitations provision constitutes a condition on the waiver of sovereign immunity' and defines the court's jurisdiction, and in Block v. North Dakota the Court explicitly confirmed that failure to comply with § 2409a(g) deprives courts of jurisdiction to inquire into the merits. The petitioners' reliance on modern claim-processing rule distinctions cannot override the clear structural reality that Congress conditioned its waiver on the 12-year deadline — a condition reinforced by the explicit statutory carve-out for States, which demonstrates Congress knew how to create exceptions and chose to create only one, leaving the limitations period otherwise absolute. Applying equitable tolling or waiver to this jurisdictional condition would impermissibly expand the United States' consent to suit beyond what Congress authorized, violating the foundational textualist and originalist principle that waivers of sovereign immunity must be strictly construed in favor of the sovereign.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Quiet Title Act's 12-year limitations period in 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g) is embedded within Congress's carefully circumscribed waiver of sovereign immunity, and the text, context, and historical treatment of the provision collectively demonstrate that Congress intended it as a jurisdictional condition on the government's consent to be sued. While I acknowledge the Court's modern framework in Boechler and Kwai Fun Wong demands a clear statement before treating a deadline as jurisdictional, the QTA's structure — explicitly carving out an exception for States while imposing the 12-year bar on all other civil actions — reflects a deliberate congressional calibration of the waiver's scope that distinguishes it from ordinary claim-processing rules. The sovereign immunity context matters: when Congress waives immunity conditionally, courts should construe the conditions strictly rather than invite equitable end-runs around the government's carefully negotiated consent. Permitting tolling and waiver here would effectively rewrite the terms on which the United States agreed to be sued, undermining the separation of powers principle that only Congress may define the scope of sovereign immunity waivers.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under the Court's modern framework established in Boechler, Henderson v. Shinseki, and Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center, a statutory deadline carries jurisdictional significance only when traditional tools of statutory construction 'plainly show' Congress imbued it with such consequences — a clear statement rule that the QTA's § 2409a(g) does not satisfy merely by being embedded within a sovereign immunity waiver. The government's argument conflates the jurisdictional nature of the sovereign immunity waiver itself with the procedural time limit governing when claims must be filed; these are analytically distinct inquiries, and the presence of a limitations period within a waiver statute does not automatically transform that period into a jurisdictional bar under Reed Elsevier and Arbaugh v. Y&H Corp. From a pragmatic standpoint, treating the deadline as jurisdictional produces severe and inequitable consequences for landowners — often rural, indigenous, or otherwise vulnerable communities in the western United States where federal land dominance creates inherent informational asymmetries — who may not discover the government's adverse claim within 12 years through no fault of their own, and Congress's explicit carve-out for States suggests the limitations period operates more like a claim-processing rule subject to equitable adjustment. Classifying § 2409a(g) as a non-jurisdictional claim-processing rule preserves courts' ability to apply equitable tolling in appropriate circumstances while still respecting the government's sovereign immunity, consistent with the Court's trajectory in Kwai Fun Wong.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under the Court's modern framework articulated in cases like Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center and Boechler v. Commissioner, a statutory time limit is jurisdictional only when Congress has clearly designated it as such — a 'magic words' requirement that prevents courts from casually labeling procedural rules as jurisdiction-stripping. While the government's argument that sovereign immunity waivers must be strictly construed has historical force, as reflected in Block v. North Dakota and Mottaz, the more recent trajectory of the Court's jurisprudence — particularly Boechler's treatment of Brockamp as a merits-stage equitable tolling question rather than a jurisdictional one — strongly suggests the Court has moved away from treating every time limit embedded in a sovereign immunity waiver as automatically jurisdictional. The QTA's text in § 2409a(g) does not explicitly designate the 12-year period as jurisdictional, and the statute's inclusion of a specific exception for States actually cuts both ways: it shows Congress knew how to carve out exceptions, suggesting the limitations period is a carefully calibrated claim-processing rule rather than an absolute jurisdictional bar. Treating the deadline as a non-jurisdictional claim-processing rule produces a more workable and coherent statutory scheme, allowing courts to apply equitable doctrines in appropriate circumstances without wholesale abandoning the government's legitimate interest in repose.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Applying the Court's modern clear-statement rule established in Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center and reinforced in Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, Congress must 'speak clearly' to imbue a procedural deadline with jurisdictional consequences — and the QTA's 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g) does not expressly refer to subject-matter jurisdiction or speak in unmistakably jurisdictional terms. The government's argument that sovereign immunity waivers automatically render embedded time limits jurisdictional conflates the waiver itself with the conditions Congress attaches to it; as Kwai Fun Wong (575 U.S. 402) demonstrates, even time limits within sovereign immunity waivers can be non-jurisdictional claim-processing rules subject to equitable tolling. Furthermore, the textual structure of § 2409a(g) — which carves out an explicit exception for States — suggests Congress was legislating procedurally rather than defining the outer bounds of judicial power, since a true jurisdictional limit would not ordinarily admit of such ad hoc statutory exceptions. As a textualist, I am bound to apply the plain meaning of the statute as written, and absent a clear congressional designation of this deadline as jurisdictional, courts retain authority to apply equitable doctrines like tolling.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the Court's modern framework established in Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center, Reed Elsevier, and Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, a statutory time limit carries jurisdictional consequences only when traditional tools of statutory construction 'plainly show' that Congress imbued the deadline with jurisdictional significance through clear statement in text, context, and historical treatment. The QTA's 12-year limitation in § 2409a(g) does not expressly invoke subject-matter jurisdiction or speak in unmistakably jurisdictional terms, and the government's argument that sovereign immunity waivers automatically render all embedded conditions jurisdictional conflates the waiver itself with the procedural mechanics of enforcing it. While I take seriously the government's structural argument that time limits within sovereign immunity waivers have historically received jurisdictional treatment — and the precedent and practice factor from Musacchio v. United States gives me some pause — the Court's consistent post-2010 course correction against mislabeling claim-processing rules as jurisdictional, combined with the absence of a clear congressional statement designating this deadline as jurisdictional, counsels in favor of treating § 2409a(g) as a non-jurisdictional claim-processing rule subject to equitable tolling and waiver.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Court's modern framework established in Arbaugh, Reed Elsevier, Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center, and Boechler, a statutory time limit carries jurisdictional weight only when traditional tools of statutory construction 'plainly show' Congress imbued it with jurisdictional consequences — and Congress need not incant magic words, but the indication must be clear from text, context, and historical treatment. The QTA's 12-year limitation in § 2409a(g) does not expressly speak in jurisdictional terms or reference subject-matter jurisdiction, and critically, as the Court held in Kwai Fun Wong, 'it makes no difference' that a time bar conditions a waiver of sovereign immunity — the sovereign immunity context alone does not automatically render a limitations period jurisdictional under the modern framework. The government's position conflates the jurisdictional nature of the underlying sovereign immunity waiver with the separate question of whether the limitations period itself is jurisdictional, a conflation the Court has explicitly rejected. Consistent with Boechler's textualist methodology requiring a clear statement before stripping courts of equitable flexibility, the QTA's limitations period is better characterized as a claim-processing rule subject to tolling and waiver.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under the Court's modern framework established in Sebelius v. Auburn Regional Medical Center and refined in Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, a statutory deadline carries jurisdictional weight only when traditional tools of statutory construction 'plainly show' Congress imbued it with jurisdictional consequences — a demanding standard the QTA's § 2409a(g) does not clearly satisfy. While the government argues that sovereign immunity waivers must be strictly construed and that the time limit is an integral condition of that waiver, the Court's post-Irwin jurisprudence has moved decisively away from treating every procedural limitation embedded in a sovereign immunity waiver as automatically jurisdictional, instead requiring a clear statement. The QTA's text does not expressly speak in jurisdictional terms or reference subject-matter jurisdiction, and the mere structural proximity of the limitations period to the waiver provision is insufficient under Boechler to transform a claim-processing rule into a jurisdictional bar. From a practical consequences standpoint — which my background as a public defender reinforces — treating this deadline as an absolute jurisdictional strip without possibility of equitable tolling produces harsh results for landowners who may have had no reasonable opportunity to discover the federal government's adverse claim within the 12-year window, undermining the equal protection principles that should govern access to courts.

Stanton, represented by Pacific Legal Foundation, argue that the QTA's statute of limitations is a non-jurisdictional claim-processing rule rather than a jurisdictional bar. Under this interpretation, the 12-year deadline would be subject to equitable doctrines such as tolling, waiver, and forfeiture, allowing courts to consider untimely claims under appropriate circumstances. Prelogar, argues that the QTA's 12-year limitations period is jurisdictional in nature because it is embedded within the statute that waives the federal government's sovereign immunity. The government contends that when Congress conditions a waiver of sovereign immunity on a time limitation, that condition is necessarily jurisdictional and must be strictly construed. Because the QTA is the exclusive means by which private parties may sue the United States to quiet title, the timeliness requirement defines the outer boundary of the court's subject-matter jurisdiction, and courts lack authority to apply equitable tolling or other exceptions to extend the filing deadline.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas makes the strongest case for the respondent by arguing that the structural placement of the limitations period within the sovereign immunity waiver itself supplies the requisite clarity — essentially that the sovereign immunity context is self-evidencing of jurisdictional intent. But this argument proves too much: as Justice Barrett correctly observes, it conflates the threshold question of whether the United States has consented to suit at all with the distinct question of whether a procedural condition on that suit carries jurisdictional consequences in the technical sense. Wong directly confronted this precise argument in the FTCA context and rejected it, holding that embedding a time bar within a sovereign immunity waiver does not automatically render it jurisdictional absent a clear congressional statement — and I see no principled basis for treating the QTA differently from the FTCA on this structural point. I would write narrowly, holding only that § 2409a(g) is a non-jurisdictional claim-processing rule under the Arbaugh/Wong framework, leaving undisturbed the broader sovereign immunity canon and expressly reserving whether equitable tolling is available on the specific facts, which preserves institutional legitimacy by not overreaching beyond what this case requires.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that Wong controls because the FTCA's limitations period was similarly embedded within a sovereign immunity waiver and yet was held non-jurisdictional is the most formidable challenge I face, and I have wrestled seriously with it. But I remain unpersuaded for a reason none of my colleagues have fully addressed: the FTCA's limitations period in Wong was located in a separate provision from the waiver itself, whereas the QTA's § 2409a(g) places the 12-year bar within the same subsection that creates the cause of action, making the time limit structurally inseparable from the consent — the sovereign has not consented to suit simpliciter and then separately imposed a procedural condition, but has consented only to suits brought within 12 years, which is a different thing entirely. Justice Kagan argues that 'shall be barred' is claim-processing language rather than jurisdictional language, but under original public meaning, when a sovereign conditions its consent to suit on a temporal limitation, the natural reading is that courts lack authority to hear claims outside that window — no magic words like 'jurisdiction' are required when the structural meaning is plain. I acknowledge the 7-2 tally weighs against me, but the strength of a legal position is not determined by vote count, and I believe the majority's approach effectively permits courts to equitably expand a sovereign immunity waiver beyond what Congress authorized, which Sherwood and Block forbid regardless of how we label the procedural mechanism.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument remains the most formidable challenge to my position, and I acknowledge that Wong does create genuine structural tension with the respondent's case — the FTCA's limitations period was similarly embedded within a sovereign immunity waiver, and the Court nonetheless found it non-jurisdictional. However, I maintain my position for one reason that I believe my colleagues have not fully answered: the QTA's § 2409a(g) does not merely impose a time limit on an independently existing cause of action, but rather the entire cause of action — the right to sue the United States over title to land — exists only because of the QTA itself, making the 12-year period inseparable from the consent rather than a procedural gloss upon it. Justice Thomas correctly identifies that Block v. North Dakota and Mottaz, while decided under pre-Arbaugh methodology, reflect a consistent judicial understanding that the QTA's limitations period operates as a jurisdictional boundary, and the majority's approach of dismissing these precedents as mere 'casual use' of jurisdictional language understates their doctrinal weight in the specific QTA context. I write separately to note that even if I am wrong on the jurisdictional question, the Court should proceed with extreme caution before permitting equitable tolling to expand a sovereign immunity waiver, as the strict construction canon retains independent force at the remedial stage even if it does not resolve the threshold jurisdictional characterization.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most formidable argument — that the structural placement of the limitations period within the sovereign immunity waiver itself supplies the requisite clarity — remains unpersuasive after full deliberation, and I find Justice Barrett's analysis dispositive: Wong directly rejected the proposition that embedding a time bar within a sovereign immunity waiver automatically renders it jurisdictional, and accepting Justice Thomas's structural inference would effectively overrule Wong sub silentio without acknowledging that consequence. The state-plaintiff carve-out in § 2409a(g) is particularly telling from my perspective as someone attentive to real-world impacts — Congress was plainly calibrating procedural conditions for different categories of litigants, which is the hallmark of a claim-processing framework, not defining the outer boundary of judicial power, since true jurisdictional grants do not bend to enumerated exceptions for particular plaintiff classes. Justice Alito's concession that Wong 'creates genuine tension' with the respondent's position is telling — it is not merely tension but a direct precedential obstacle that the respondent cannot surmount without asking us to distinguish the QTA from the FTCA on grounds that are structurally indistinguishable. For vulnerable rural landowners who may not discover federal encroachments for decades, the practical stakes of foreclosing equitable tolling entirely reinforce my conviction that absent unmistakably clear congressional language — not structural inference — we should not strip courts of the power to hear their claims.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas makes the strongest opposing argument — that the structural placement of the limitations period within the sovereign immunity waiver itself supplies the requisite clarity, and that the explicit state-plaintiff carve-out demonstrates Congress understood the 12-year period as a jurisdictional boundary. But this argument proves too much: as Justice Barrett correctly observes, the presence of enumerated exceptions actually cuts against jurisdictional characterization, since true subject-matter jurisdiction grants do not typically admit of such legislatively crafted exceptions. More fundamentally, Wong directly confronted and rejected the argument that embedding a time bar within a sovereign immunity waiver statute automatically renders it jurisdictional — the Court held that the sovereign immunity context does not substitute for the clear statement Congress must provide, and Justice Thomas's position would effectively overrule Wong sub silentio without acknowledging that it does so. The QTA's text speaks to when claims 'shall be barred,' which is the language of claim-processing rules, not the language of jurisdictional grants, and I am not persuaded that structural placement alone can supply what the text itself omits.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most refined argument — that the QTA's structural placement of the limitations period within the waiver provision itself, combined with the state-plaintiff carve-out, supplies the requisite clarity — remains the strongest challenge to my position, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for the same reason Justice Barrett articulates so precisely: Wong directly confronted a sovereign immunity waiver's embedded time bar and held that structural placement alone cannot substitute for the clear congressional statement Arbaugh requires. As a textualist, I cannot accept that structural inference does the work of explicit text; the QTA says claims 'shall be barred,' which is the language of claim-processing rules, and if Congress intended to strip courts of jurisdiction it knew how to say so. Justice Thomas's reading of the state-plaintiff carve-out as confirming jurisdictional intent actually undermines his own position — true jurisdictional grants defining the outer boundary of federal court power do not admit of enumerated congressional exceptions for particular plaintiff categories, as that would be structurally anomalous. I maintain my position for the petitioner with increased confidence given the convergence of textualist methodology, Wong's controlling precedent, and the structural anomaly Justice Thomas's reading creates.
